book_title: Chapter 4: The Battlefield — Rivals, Switching Costs & Moat Reality
question: Who does Creative Newtech really compete with, what stops its vendors and customers from going around it, and how much of its profit rests on one licence it does not own?

epigraph.quote: Honeywell has a very small team of 4 people who do the licensing business, but they get a large revenue into that place.
epigraph.author: Ketan Patel, Chairman & MD, Creative Newtech, Q4 FY26 earnings call, 15 May 2026

web_blocks.text: India's technology distribution industry has three layers, and Creative Newtech sits in the middle one while trying to climb into the third. The first layer is broadline distribution, where scale is everything: Redington booked consolidated FY26 revenue of ₹1,19,347 Cr, Savex Technologies about ₹35,301 Cr of gross revenue, and Rashi Peripherals ₹15,827 Cr [22][26][23]. They carry the big principals, HP, Dell, Lenovo, Apple, Samsung and Cisco, and earn operating margins of roughly 2% to 3.5%. The second layer is specialist and market-entry distribution, where a distributor takes on brands that the giants do not want to build from scratch; this is where Creative's ₹2,704.62 Cr of FY26 revenue mostly sits [15]. The third layer is brand ownership and licensing, where the margin pool is different in kind: CP Plus, India's leading surveillance brand, reported a 28.8% gross margin and 13.7% EBITDA margin in FY26, against distributors' low single digits [24]. Creative's strategy is to use the second layer's logistics to feed the third layer's economics. The question for this chapter is how defensible each layer is.

web_blocks.takeaway: Creative's blended 3.8% EBITDA margin sits above the broadliners' 2% to 3% only because of its brand mix, and a brand owner such as CP Plus earns three to four times as much gross margin on its own product. The business is therefore a hybrid whose profit comes from the layer it only partly owns. [15][22][23][24][26]

web_blocks.text: Three things stand out. First, scale: Creative's revenue is about 2.3% of Redington's and 17% of Rashi's [15][22][23]. It cannot win on purchasing power, and Ketan Patel's own explanation of why Make-in-India vendors pay a higher percentage margin, that these vendors are much smaller, points the same way [16]. Second, cash conversion: even Rashi, the second-largest listed IT distributor, reported operating cash outflows of ₹114.6 Cr, ₹102.0 Cr and ₹299.2 Cr in FY23, FY24 and FY25 while earning profit each year, and only turned positive at ₹113.7 Cr in FY26 [23]. Creative's own FY25 operating cash flow was ₹21.86 Cr positive and FY26 negative ₹271.88 Cr [15]. Negative cash conversion in growth years is therefore the industry norm, not a Creative quirk. Third, the margin gap: CP Plus's 121 debtor days and 138 creditor days show that a brand owner can have the same long receivable cycle and still be funded by suppliers, which is the structure Creative's brand road is trying to copy [24].

web_blocks.title: Disintermediation: who can go around Creative, and what does it add?

web_blocks.text: The risk that a vendor skips the distributor takes three forms in this industry, and each has evidence on both sides. The first is direct selling by the vendor or by a marketplace. Channel Dive's June 2026 report notes that the three largest cloud providers have become de facto distributors, that distributors may start billing end customers directly, and that vendors are concentrating around fewer distributors, which Omdia's analyst says will widen the gap between the largest platforms and smaller distributors because platform capability costs tens, if not hundreds, of millions of dollars [27]. Creative is on the wrong side of that scale line. The second form is vendor exit: Savex lost Samsung as a key principal and CRISIL still rated it AA, but only because other principals replaced the volume [26]. The third is regulatory orphaning: Aditya Infotech was national distributor for Dahua for 16 years, and when India refused to certify Chinese-chipset cameras its Dahua business contracted by 80% [25].

What Creative adds is real, but narrow. In the market-entry model it brings a brand that has no Indian presence into 10,000+ partners, 31+ branches and 18 warehouses, handles import and bonded storage, pre-sales demos and after-sales, and in the AR's words trains resellers at the ground level [15]. That value is highest for small and new brands, which cannot justify a direct team, and lowest for brands that reach scale. Creative's own FY26 additions, Kaspersky, PDRL, EIZO, Matrix and Sparsh, are exactly of this kind [15][16]. The risk is graduation: successful brands tend to go direct. The investor should treat the market-entry road as an annuity that must be re-earned every time a brand grows up, and the audited segment margin of 3.8% gives little cushion if one of the bigger lines leaves. We assess the chance that at least one top-five principal reduces or removes Creative's role within three years at about one in three, and the chance that this alone breaks the business at below one in ten, because the brand road and enterprise projects diversify the earnings.

web_blocks.region_era: United States and global markets, wireless-device distribution and logistics, 2011 to 2012
web_blocks.mechanism: A thin-margin distributor dependent on a few vendors and customers lost its largest customer and saw a key handset vendor, Research in Motion, falter within months. It carried working-capital debt and, so far as the sources show, no consumer brand of its own to fall back on, so a vendor shock turned directly into a sale to a larger distributor.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: 2011 revenue about $5.2 billion and about 4,000 employees worldwide; RIM was about 10% of its distribution business; the lost Cricket account had been 6.8 million devices in 2011; February 2012 earnings guidance cut and March 2012 layoffs; a 2-cent-per-share second-quarter loss flagged and prior guidance withdrawn on 2 July 2012; agreed sale to Ingram Micro for about $650 million in cash plus roughly $190 million of assumed debt.
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: Scale and a 112-million-device throughput did not protect BrightPoint once two concentrated relationships failed together. For Creative the analogue is the Honeywell licence and a handful of principals: the brand road is the shock absorber that BrightPoint lacked, but it is also a single, terminable dependency. [28]

web_blocks.title: The Honeywell licence: term, renewal, and what is at stake

web_blocks.takeaway: Management has given three different renewal dates in twelve months. The original term to 31 December 2020 plus one five-year roll fits December 2025; the later dates fit only if later-added territories or categories carry their own five-year clocks, which is our inference because the agreement is not public. December 2025 has passed with no disclosed renewal event and management still points to March 2027, so the disclosures are comforting on intent and thin on terms. [16][19][21]

web_blocks.text: The contractual economics are favourable. The royalty expense in the audited notes was ₹5.96 Cr in FY26 against ₹5.88 Cr in FY25, a rise of 1.4% while the brand segment's revenue rose 41% [15]. That is 1.6% of ₹369.61 Cr of Honeywell revenue and 4.7% of the ₹126.29 Cr brand segment result [15][16]. Ketan Patel's explanation is that the royalty is a fixed-style amount that rises only when a territory is added [21]. The same fact is the risk. A licensor who sees a licensee grow Honeywell sales by about 45% in a year (₹255.17 Cr to ₹369.61 Cr) while paying a flat fee has a clear incentive to reset the terms at renewal. As an illustration, not a forecast, a royalty of 5% of Honeywell sales would cost ₹18.5 Cr, about ₹12.5 Cr more than FY26, equal to 15% of the year's ₹81.76 Cr pre-tax profit [15]. Honeywell also controls design through its design language system and can reallocate categories among licensees, as management says it did with air purifiers [21]. And Creative has no Honeywell rights in the United States, one reason it launched WOZOYO [16][17].

The corporate backdrop adds uncertainty rather than direct risk. Ketan Patel told the May 2026 call that Honeywell was splitting into five companies [16]. Honeywell's own October 2025 announcement describes separating Aerospace and Solstice Advanced Materials from a remaining three-segment automation business, which is a three-way split, not five (see Honeywell's segment-structure release). The difference in count is minor, but the uncertainty it covers is not: which successor entity owns the consumer-products trademark programme, and whether its licensing team inherits Creative's five-year renewal cycle, is not stated in any document we read. Management says it expects renewal and has the best scorecard rating on record, 4.8 out of 5 [21]. Our probability assessment: roughly 65% that the licence renews on broadly current terms, about 25% that it renews with materially higher cost or narrower scope, and about 10% that a major category or territory is lost, within the next 18 months.

Why does this matter so much? Because the brand road is where the profit sits. Audited FY26 segment results put 59% of the ₹213.58 Cr total in the Brand Business on 14% of revenue [15]. The CFO expects brand-business EBITDA of about 13% [16], which on ₹380.86 Cr of brand revenue is roughly ₹49.5 Cr, or 48% of the company's ₹103.95 Cr EBITDA [15]. That is our arithmetic on management's expected margin, not an audited segment EBITDA. Management says the Hong Kong base carries no tax on the brand road [16], but only 77.5% belongs to Creative's shareholders: the non-controlling interest took ₹8.42 Cr, 12% of consolidated profit after tax [15]. Management plans to separate the brand business in two to three years, but not within the next fifteen months [16]. A separated brand company would hold the licence on its own, and the market-entry company would be left with the thin-margin base.

Regulation has created a genuine moat in surveillance, and it is the most interesting new fact in the file. India's electronics ministry introduced essential-requirement norms for CCTV cameras in April 2024 and gave a two-year transition; from April 2026 internet-connected cameras need STQC certification, which in practice excludes Chinese-chipset products [25]. Chinese brands held a third of CCTV sales in 2024; Indian brands held over 80% by February 2026, with CP Plus rising to 45% to 50% from 20% to 25%; and 507 camera models were certified [25]. Management's reading is that surveillance and drones are 'national security' categories that foreign players will never be allowed to dominate [16]. Creative has positioned itself as the pan-India distributor of Matrix and Sparsh, two of the four major Indian STQC-approved players (company decks call the arrangements exclusive; the releases say partnership), and is buying Infinova India, which fell from ₹38 Cr to ₹32 Cr in sales for want of STQC certification [18][17]. The STQC criteria Ketan Patel set out are demanding: no Chinese-origin components, Indian software and board files, and no Chinese owner or director [17].

But a regulatory moat protects the product, not the distributor. Any Indian distributor can sign an STQC-certified brand, and the biggest beneficiary so far is the brand owner CP Plus, not a distributor. The same rule is a shock for Creative's Dahua line, which the annual report lists as video door phones and which sits in a brand family that lost its main market [15][25]. Component costs have risen 15% to 20% for the switch away from Chinese chipsets [25], and management says memory, storage and CPU costs rose 30% to 40% in 2026, with Red Sea freight moving from $1,500-$1,700 to $7,500-$8,000 and about half of the ₹137.60 Cr of Honeywell sales outside India exposed to the Middle East [16]. Import duties, production-linked incentives and export entitlements (₹4.84 Cr, down from ₹8.28 Cr in FY25) are second-order here, and certification and inspection spending of ₹0.87 Cr and ₹0.82 Cr in FY26 is small [15].

web_blocks.text: Our assessment is a narrow, localized moat. For the Market Entry Specialist road, which supplies 86% of revenue and 41% of gross profit, we see no durable moat: about 80% likely that margins stay in the 3% to 4% band regardless of growth, because vendors, rivals and marketplaces all set the price [15]. For the Honeywell franchise, the moat is real but contractual: a licensor can reset it, and the evidence of reset risk, a flat royalty on fast-growing sales, is in the audited notes. For the surveillance and drone categories the moat belongs mostly to Indian brand owners and to whoever owns them, which is why the Infinova acquisition matters more than the Matrix and Sparsh distribution agreements. Over a five-year horizon we think it is more likely than not, about 60%, that Creative's blended earnings quality improves as brand share rises, and about one in four that a licence reset or vendor loss pushes them back. Both outcomes are plausible, and the numbers do not yet settle which is likelier.

book_paragraphs: Let me draw you the map before we argue about the territory. India's technology distribution trade has three floors. On the ground floor are the giants. Redington booked ₹1,19,347 Cr of revenue in FY26, Savex about ₹35,301 Cr, and Rashi Peripherals ₹15,827 Cr. They carry HP, Dell, Lenovo, Apple and Samsung and live on operating margins of two to three and a half percent. On the first floor sit the specialists, the distributors who take brands the giants do not want to nurse through their early years. That is where Creative's ₹2,705 Cr sits. On the top floor are the brand owners: CP Plus earned a 28.8 percent gross margin and 13.7 percent EBITDA margin in FY26. Creative wants to ride the lift from the first floor to the third, and every number in this chapter is a question about whether the lift is working.

Start with size, because it decides who sets prices. Creative's revenue is two and a quarter percent of Redington's and seventeen percent of Rashi's. It cannot out-buy anyone. When Ketan Patel explained on the 15 May 2026 call why Make-in-India vendors give a higher percentage margin, the reason he gave was that 'their size is much smaller', which is a polite way of saying that the big names are already taken. That honesty is useful. It tells you the company is not pretending to have scale advantages; it is choosing niches. The question is whether niches stay profitable once they are discovered, and distribution history says they rarely do. A category that earns a fat margin for a year attracts another distributor in the second year and a direct deal from the vendor in the third.

The cash picture of this industry should humble anyone who judges Creative's FY26 outflow in isolation. Rashi Peripherals, the second-largest listed IT distributor, reported negative operating cash flow of ₹114.6 Cr in FY23, ₹102.0 Cr in FY24 and ₹299.2 Cr in FY25 while reporting profits each year, and turned positive at ₹113.7 Cr only in FY26. Redington's own management warned on its May 2026 call that working capital could go up because it may have to give more credit or stock excess to avoid stock-outs. So a growing distributor consuming cash is normal. What is not normal is relying on a single year of supplier-funded inflow to prove otherwise. When you read a distributor's cash flow, take eighteen months at a time, as we did in the last chapter, and compare the shape of the cycle, not the single quarter.

Now think about who can go around Creative, because every middleman lives with that fear. There are three ways it happens. A vendor can sell direct, as Samsung did when it left Savex as a key principal. A marketplace can become the distributor, as the hyperscalers did to Ingram Micro in cloud, where Omdia's analyst says vendors are concentrating around fewer distributors and the platform cost, 'tens, if not hundreds, of millions of dollars', widens the gap between giants and smaller players. Or the regulator can orphan a brand, as happened to Aditya Infotech, which was Dahua's national distributor for sixteen years and watched that business shrink by eighty percent. Creative has a pinch of all three exposures: it signed Dahua in FY26, it sells through Amazon, and its smaller brands are the sort that graduate to direct. I weigh the risk at about one in three over three years for at least one top-five principal changing its terms.

What does Creative add that a vendor cannot easily replace? I would say three things, in rising order of value. First, import and warehousing: 18 warehouses, a bonded mother facility in Bhiwandi and an AEO-T2 customs status make arrival and clearance predictable. Second, channel reach: 10,000-plus partners and branches in 31 cities who know how to sell a monitor or a cable. Third, brand-building judgement: the one thing Ketan Patel says took seven years to learn with Honeywell and which he now believes he can do in three and a half. The first two are replicable by anyone with capital. The third is the real asset, and it is a skill rather than a contract. That is why I give more weight to WOZOYO's early numbers than to any distribution agreement, and why I treat the first two as a necessary but unexceptional base.

Let me tell you the story the BrightPoint history teaches, because I want you to hold it beside Creative. BrightPoint was an Indianapolis wireless-device distributor with $5.2 billion of 2011 revenue and 112 million devices handled. In early 2012 it lost its biggest customer, Cricket, whose volume was 6.8 million devices, and one of its main vendors, Research in Motion, accounting for about ten percent of its distribution business, began to fail. It cut guidance in February, laid off staff in March, and in early July withdrew guidance and agreed to be sold to Ingram Micro for roughly $650 million in cash plus $190 million of debt. Size did not save it. Two concentrated relationships moved together, debt stood in the way of a rescue, and as far as the record shows it had no brand of its own. Creative does have a brand road, and that matters; but the Honeywell licence is a single point of failure of the same kind.

So let us read the licence the way a lawyer and an analyst would together. The prospectus tells us the original agreement was dated 4 December 2015 and ran to 31 December 2020, with royalty on net sales. Ketan Patel told the 16 May 2025 call that 'the license agreement is kind of a perpetuity if you pay the minimum guarantee', renewing every five years. Then he gave three different renewal dates in twelve months: December 2025 on that call, 'end of '27' on 12 November 2025, and 'March 2027' on 15 May 2026. All three could be true only if different territories or categories sit on different five-year clocks, and none can be checked because the agreement itself is not public. December 2025 has since passed with no disclosed renewal event. When he says 'we are very sure that the Honeywell license will get renewed after March '27', I believe he believes it. I also note that the licensor's trademark team was six people in his 2025 telling and four in his 2026 telling, and that the licensor has a corporate split to complete.

Here is the part that should hold your attention. The royalty line in the audited notes was ₹5.96 Cr in FY26 against ₹5.88 Cr the year before, an increase of 1.4 percent while Brand Business revenue rose 41 percent. Think about what that means from Honeywell's side of the table. A licensee grows the brand by forty percent a year on a fixed-style fee, and the licensor's trademark team, which Ketan says is four people, sees that fee equal to 1.6 percent of sales. At renewal, would you ask for the same fee? I would not. As an illustration only, a royalty of five percent of Honeywell sales would be ₹18.5 Cr, ₹12.5 Cr more than FY26, or fifteen percent of the year's pre-tax profit. My probability range is about 65 percent for renewal on current terms, 25 percent for renewal with higher cost or narrower scope, and 10 percent for a loss of an important category or territory.

The stakes are visible if you do one calculation. Management expects the brand business to earn about thirteen percent EBITDA. On ₹381 Cr of FY26 brand revenue that is roughly ₹49.5 Cr, about 48 percent of the company's ₹103.95 Cr of EBITDA, from fourteen percent of sales. Of that, only 77.5 percent belongs to Creative's shareholders, since the Hong Kong subsidiary has a minority that took ₹8.42 Cr, or 12 percent, of profit after tax. Ketan has said the brand business will be separated in two to three years, though not for fifteen months, and that 'any brand which is not doing INR1,000 crores is not a brand'. Put those together and you see a company whose most valuable asset is a licence, whose management wants to hive it off, and whose remainder would be a distribution business earning three to four percent gross margin.

Regulation looks like a friend here, and I want you to be careful with that thought. From April 2026, internet-connected CCTV cameras in India need STQC certification, which excludes Chinese chipsets. Chinese brands had a third of the market in 2024; by February 2026 Indian brands held more than eighty percent, and CP Plus alone held 45 to 50 percent. Ketan Patel believes surveillance is a category where 'the government will never allow a foreign company to come in', and so he partnered with Matrix and Sparsh and is buying Infinova. The thesis makes sense. But whose moat is it? A moat that any rival distributor can cross by signing a certified brand protects the brand owner, not the distributor. The regulator creates a gate; it does not hand the gatekeeper's keys to Creative. I would rate this protection medium and localized, with Infinova the one asset that could make it Creative's own.

Is there anything that caps gross margin and anything that lifts it? The cap is plain: pass-through pricing in a business with 2.09 percent enterprise gross margin in FY25, broadline operating margins of two to three and a half percent, and input costs, memory, storage and processors, which Ketan says rose thirty to forty percent in 2026. The lifts are mix, not magic. Brand share rose from 14 percent of revenue in FY26 to 19 percent in Q2 FY27, taking consolidated gross margin from 7.90 percent to 11.34 percent. WOZOYO sold about $2.2 million in its first months, with Amazon advertising near half of sales; Ketan says it must fall to 12 to 14 percent at a million dollars. Brand EBITDA margin of 13 percent and a path to 18 percent are the prize. I would say the cap is structural and the lift is plausible, which is an unsatisfying but honest summary.

My assessment of the moat is narrow and localized. For the market-entry road, with 86 percent of revenue and 41 percent of gross profit, I see no durable moat; I would put the chance that margins stay between three and four percent at about 80 percent. For the Honeywell franchise the moat is real but rented. For surveillance the moat belongs to Indian brand owners, and Creative's best route to share in it is ownership, which is why Infinova deserves more of your attention than the distribution agreements. Over five years I think it is about 60 percent likely that earnings quality improves as brand share rises and about one in four that a licence reset or a vendor loss pushes it back. Hold both numbers loosely. The next chapters will test them against profits and cash, and the renewal in March 2027 will be the cleanest test of all.

Before you move on, do the homework in the External Learning Hub. Read the Q4 FY26 and Q2 FY27 transcripts, not the summaries, and underline every place where Ketan Patel and Ajit Thakur disagree with the slide deck in tone. Open the annual report to the segment note and royalty line and draw the ₹100 waterfall yourself. Watch the founders' interviews and ask whether they talk about the licence as an asset they own or one they rent. Read Redington's call and Rashi's deck to see what a mature distributor's working capital looks like. Then compare the CP Plus presentation with Creative's brand segment and decide whether a ₹380 Cr brand segment at 33 percent is a business or a profitable chapter in someone else's book. A moat assessment is an opinion; the primary sources are the evidence.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: I started this chapter expecting to write about competitors and ended up writing about a contract. That is how it often goes with distributors: the visible rivals are the ones you can name, and the invisible one is the licensor or vendor whose terms you cannot see. Creative's management has been unusually frank about the thin margin and the supplier-funded cash flow. I wish the same frankness extended to the text of the Honeywell licence, because the whole brand road depends on a document the shareholder has never read.

book_callouts.title: MENTAL MODEL: WHO OWNS THE MOAT?
book_callouts.text: When a regulation, a trademark or a platform protects an industry, ask who holds the title deed. If any rival can sign the same certified brand or the same marketplace listing, the moat belongs to the brand owner or the platform. A distributor shares in it only if it owns the brand or holds an exclusive, renewable right that cannot be repriced at the licensor's whim.
